title: What Is an API? Explained with a Restaurant

scenes.narration: Your weather app does not own a single weather station. So how does it know it is raining in Nairobi right now? The answer is something you use hundreds of times a day without noticing: an API. By the end of this video, you will understand exactly what that is.

Imagine you are at a restaurant. You are hungry, but you cannot walk into the kitchen and start cooking. You also do not need to know how the kitchen works. You just need a way to ask for food and get it back. That is the waiter. You give the waiter your order, the waiter carries it to the kitchen, the kitchen prepares it, and the waiter brings your meal back.

cues.order: You give the waiter your order

scenes.narration: An API, short for Application Programming Interface, is the waiter. It is the messenger between two pieces of software. One side asks. The other side answers. And the one asking never has to see what happens inside.

cues.software: messenger between two pieces of software

scenes.narration: Now let's swap the restaurant for the real thing. The customer is your weather app. The kitchen is a weather company's server, which holds all the data. The waiter is the API. Step one is the request. Your app sends a message that says, give me the weather for Nairobi, in a format the server understands. Step two: the API receives it, checks that the request is valid, and often checks that you are allowed to ask.

Step three: the server does the work. It looks up the data and prepares an answer. Step four is the response. The API carries the answer back, usually in a format called JSON, which is simply neatly organized text: city, Nairobi. Temperature, twenty four degrees. Condition, light rain. Then your app turns that data into the icons and numbers you see.

Notice what did not happen. Your app never touched the weather company's database. It never needed to know how the data was collected. It only knew how to ask, and how to read the answer. That separation is the whole point.

visual.title: Why this design works
items: The app never touches the database
It only asks and reads the answer
Each side can change without breaking the other

cues: It only knew how to ask

scenes.narration: This is why APIs are everywhere. When you pay online, a shop talks to your bank through an API. When you log in with Google, a website talks to Google through an API. When a travel site compares flights, it asks dozens of airline APIs at once.

visual.title: APIs are everywhere
items: Log in with Google: website and Google
Comparing flights: travel site and airlines

cues: When you log in with Google
When a travel site compares flights

scenes.narration: Let's see how little code it takes. This free, public API returns a random joke. A few lines of Python ask a server across the world a question and get an answer back. What comes back is not a pretty page. It is raw data, a setup and a punchline, and apps decorate it. That is the power of an API.

visual.title: Asking an API in Python
visual.code:
import requests

url = "https://official-joke-api.appspot.com/random_joke"
data = requests.get(url).json()
print(data["setup"])
print(data["punchline"])
visual.output: Output: a setup line, then a punchline

scenes.narration: Let's recap in three points. One: an API is a messenger that lets two programs talk without seeing each other's insides. Two: it works on request and response, like ordering and receiving food. Three: almost every app you use depends on dozens of them.

visual.title: Three takeaways
items: An API is a messenger between programs
Request goes out, response comes back
Almost every app depends on APIs

cues: One: an API is a messenger
